author: independent annotator A (V35)
guide: Labels follow scratch guide v35: states understood | mostlyUnderstood | fragile | misconception | weakReasoning | insufficient.

cases.text: Idempotency is the property that repeating an operation has the same intended effect as performing it once. You need it because networks retry, users double-click, and clients time out after the server has already committed the work.
credits: repeating an operation has the same intended effect
users double-click, and clients time out
cases.notes: Near copy of the definition plus the reasons duplicates happen; both correct, so understood.

cases.text: If the same request lands twice - say the app retried after a timeout even though the server had actually finished, or someone tapped Pay two times - the end result should be as if it only happened once.
credits: repeating an operation has the same intended effect
users double-click, and clients time out
cases.notes: Same-effect-as-once plus the real-world sources of duplicates (retry after timeout, double tap), in own words.

cases.text: Think of a lift call button: mash it five times and one lift still comes. An API call should work the same way, because in real life stuff gets sent twice all the time - flaky wifi resends, impatient people double-tap, a client gives up waiting after the server already did the job.
credits: repeating an operation has the same intended effect
users double-click, and clients time out
cases.notes: Lift-button analogy carries the same-effect idea and the learner names retries, double taps and timeouts as the reason.

cases.text: Doing the same call twice, or ten times, leaves things exactly as if you'd done it once.
credits: repeating an operation has the same intended effect
cases.notes: Definition is right but nothing about why repeats happen (retries, double-clicks, timeouts after committed work).

cases.text: Idempotency is when the client automatically sends the request again if it fails, and keeps trying until the server finally answers.

misconceptions.claim: repeating an operation has the same intended effect

cases.notes: Describes the act of retrying instead of the property that a repeat has the same effect as one call - a confusion with Retry.

cases.text: It's about keeping your API clean and predictable - using the proper HTTP verbs, returning sensible status codes and documenting every endpoint so clients know what to expect.
cases.notes: Plausible API-hygiene advice that never says what happens when an operation is repeated.

cases.text: Throttling is limiting an action so it runs at most once per time window while the events keep coming. It protects expensive handlers during things like scroll, resize or pointer movement.
credits: runs at most once per time window
It protects expensive handlers during scroll,
cases.notes: Near copy of both the definition and the purpose; correct and complete.

cases.text: Heavy scroll handler runs once per interval, not every event.
credits: runs at most once per time window
It protects expensive handlers during scroll,
cases.notes: Terse but states the once-per-interval cap while events keep firing and that it shields a costly scroll handler.

cases.text: Like a bus that leaves every ten minutes no matter how many people keep turning up: while the mouse is moving or the window is being dragged bigger, your costly callback gets a turn only once per slot, so it doesn't choke the page.
credits: runs at most once per time window
It protects expensive handlers during scroll,
cases.notes: Bus analogy gives the fixed-rate cap during continuing events and the protection of a costly callback during pointer/resize activity.

cases.text: Throttling waits until the user has completely stopped scrolling and then runs the handler a single time after everything goes quiet. That's the whole trick.

misconceptions.claim: once per time window while events continue

cases.notes: Wait-for-quiet-then-run-once is debouncing; throttling runs periodically while events continue.

cases.text: Throttling means the function only fires once per interval however many events come in. The reason is that JavaScript is single-threaded, so without it the events would pile up, overflow the call stack and crash the tab.
credits: runs at most once per time window
cases.notes: Definition is right, but the reason given (call-stack overflow from single-threading) is a buzzword non-sequitur instead of protecting expensive handlers.

cases.text: Debouncing means the function can only run once every X milliseconds while you're typing, so it fires on a steady schedule the whole time.

misconceptions.claim: until a burst of events has been quiet

cases.notes: A fixed once-per-interval rate during typing is throttling; debouncing waits for the burst to go quiet.

cases.text: basically you put a cap on it so while somebody keeps hammering keys the search goes off at a fixed rate, like one call every half second max

misconceptions.claim: until a burst of events has been quiet

cases.notes: Same throttling-style fixed rate while keys are still being pressed; no waiting for a pause.

cases.text: I'm fairly sure it's a rate cap: no matter how fast the events come in, the handler goes off at most once per interval, even while the typing is still happening.

misconceptions.claim: until a burst of events has been quiet

cases.notes: Hedged version of the same confusion: periodic firing during the burst instead of after it goes quiet.

cases.text: It's like an elevator door: each time someone else steps in, the countdown restarts, and it only shuts once nobody has come in for a few seconds. Same with a search box - you fire the lookup after the person pauses typing, not on every letter, so the heavy work doesn't run constantly.
credits: until a burst of events has been quiet
avoids firing expensive work for every keystroke
cases.notes: Elevator analogy captures the reset-until-quiet delay, and the search-box part gives the purpose of not doing heavy work per keystroke.

cases.text: i think it's something about waiting a little before running a function? like so it doesn't do too much work maybe
cases.notes: Gestures at waiting and saving work but never says the wait is until events stop; too vague to trust.

cases.text: Authentication is where the app checks what you're allowed to do, like whether you can edit a post or only look at it.

misconceptions.claim: verifying who a user or service is

cases.notes: Describes deciding permissions, which is authorization, not verifying identity.

cases.text: It decides your permissions - admin vs normal user, which pages you can open, that kind of thing.

misconceptions.claim: verifying who a user or service is

cases.notes: Same confusion: permissions and roles instead of establishing who the user is.

cases.text: Obviously authentication is the permissions layer: once the system has your role, it works out exactly which actions and resources you're allowed.

misconceptions.claim: verifying who a user or service is

cases.notes: Confidently equates authentication with the permission check (authorization).

cases.text: Think of a bouncer checking your ID at the door: it's only about proving you really are who you claim to be - password, face scan, a code texted to your phone. The app has to be sure of that before it lets you near anything.
credits: verifying who a user or service is
the system needs a trustworthy identity
cases.notes: Bouncer analogy gives identity verification and that a trustworthy identity must come before any access.

cases.text: Proving you are who you say you are, e.g. logging in with a password.
credits: verifying who a user or service is
cases.notes: Identity verification is right, but it does not say a trusted identity is needed before access is granted.

cases.text: Okay so, once the system already knows who you are (that part's the login step), authorization is the separate question of what you're actually allowed to touch. And just being you doesn't automatically mean you can do something - which honestly surprised me - every single request for a specific thing, like deleting this file or viewing that report, gets checked on its own, every time.
credits: deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed
Identity alone is not permission.
authorization still happens per action/resource.
cases.notes: Rambling but gives all three ideas: deciding what a known identity may do, identity is not permission, and a check per action/resource.

cases.text: It's simple: authorization happens once, when you log in. After you've proven who you are you're trusted, so you can basically do anything in the app for the rest of the session.

misconceptions.claim: Identity alone is not permission.
authorization still happens per action/resource.

cases.notes: Two wrong ideas: a proven identity grants everything, and the check happens once at login instead of per action/resource.

cases.text: authorization is checking your username and password to confirm it's really you

misconceptions.claim: deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed

cases.notes: Checking credentials to confirm identity is authentication, not deciding what that identity may do.

cases.text: Authorization is deciding what a logged-in user is allowed to do - for example regular users can read reports but only admins can delete accounts.
credits: deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed
cases.notes: Definition is right, but it misses that identity alone is not permission and that the check happens per action/resource.

cases.text: it's kind of about permissions and roles i think? like admin stuff
cases.notes: Mentions permissions and roles but never says what is being decided or for whom; too vague to trust.

cases.text: CORS is cross origin resource sharing, a security thing.
cases.notes: Only expands the acronym and calls it security; nothing about what it controls.

cases.text: I think it stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing? It has something to do with security on the web, I'm pretty sure.
cases.notes: Hedged acronym expansion plus 'web security'; no content a teacher can assess.

cases.text: So CORS, which is short for cross-origin resource sharing (a mouthful, I know), is basically one of those web security features that every developer runs into eventually. I've seen it come up a lot in tutorials and on Stack Overflow. The main thing to know is that it's related to security on the web and to resources being shared across origins, which is kind of what the name says anyway.
cases.notes: Long, but it only restates the name and says 'web security'; still no idea of who enforces what.

cases.text: CORS is a firewall on the server that blocks requests coming from other domains, and it stops everything - browsers, curl, Postman, mobile apps - from calling your API unless you whitelist them.

misconceptions.claim: A browser-enforced policy that controls whether
does not stop non-browser clients

cases.notes: Two wrong ideas: it is a server-side request blocker rather than browser-enforced read control, and it supposedly stops non-browser clients too.

cases.text: CORS is how the backend checks who is calling it - it verifies the user's identity before it agrees to send the data back.

misconceptions.claim: controls whether frontend JavaScript can read responses

cases.notes: Treats CORS as identity verification; the source says it is browser read control and explicitly not authentication.

cases.text: A JWT is an encrypted token, so nobody who grabs it can see what's inside - that's exactly why it's safe to stuff user info in there.

misconceptions.claim: claim containers, not automatically encrypted

cases.notes: Claims JWT contents are hidden by encryption; the source says JWTs are signed, not automatically encrypted.

cases.text: JWTs hide their contents. The payload part is scrambled, so only the server is able to read the user data in it.

misconceptions.claim: claim containers, not automatically encrypted

cases.notes: Same wrong idea in other words: the payload is supposedly scrambled and unreadable to the client.

cases.text: it's a login token that's encrypted, which keeps the info inside private from the browser and from anyone snooping on the traffic i believe

misconceptions.claim: claim containers, not automatically encrypted

cases.notes: Hedged, but still asserts the token's contents are encrypted and private.

cases.text: It's a small token in three dot-separated chunks - header, payload, signature. Because of the signature, whoever receives it can check the data really came from the issuer it trusts and wasn't changed, without hitting the database every time. Anyone can still decode and read the middle bit, though.
credits: compact signed token format containing claims
claims were issued by a trusted signer
cases.notes: Gives the signed three-part format and the verify-without-lookup purpose, and correctly notes it is readable (not encrypted).

cases.text: A JWT is a signed token carrying claims like the user id and expiry, and the API doesn't need a DB lookup to trust it - because it's encrypted, so the client can't read or fake anything inside.

misconceptions.claim: claim containers, not automatically encrypted

credits: compact signed token format containing claims
cases.notes: Conclusion (signed claims, trusted without a lookup) is right, but the reason offered is encryption, which contradicts the source; the signature is what makes it trustworthy.

cases.text: Hashing turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint that you can't turn back into the original. For passwords you use a purposely slow algorithm with a random salt, keep only the result, and at login you hash what they typed and compare - so the real password is never stored anywhere.
credits: one-way transformation that maps input to
uses deliberately slow, salted algorithms.
verified without storing recoverable plaintext
cases.notes: One-way fixed-size output, slow salted algorithms for passwords, and verifying without keeping the plaintext - all correct.

cases.text: you run the password through a one way function (bcrypt/argon2 - slow on purpose, plus a salt) and save what comes out. it can't be undone, the output is always the same length, and to check a login you redo it and compare. no actual passwords sitting in the db
credits: one-way transformation that maps input to
uses deliberately slow, salted algorithms.
verified without storing recoverable plaintext
cases.notes: Same three ideas in a different order and casual wording.

cases.text: Picture a meat grinder: steak becomes mince but never the other way, and every batch comes out the same size. Sites do that to passwords, adding a random pinch of salt and using a purposely slow grinder so attackers can't try billions a second, then compare at login instead of keeping the steak.
credits: one-way transformation that maps input to
uses deliberately slow, salted algorithms.
verified without storing recoverable plaintext
cases.notes: Grinder analogy carries one-way and fixed size, then slow salted hashing and compare-at-login without storing the password.

cases.text: Hashing is basically encryption for passwords: you scramble the password with a secret key and then decrypt it when the user logs in so you can compare. And you want the fastest hash you can find so logins don't lag.

misconceptions.claim: one-way transformation that maps input to
uses deliberately slow, salted algorithms.

cases.notes: Two wrong ideas: treats hashing as reversible keyed encryption, and wants a fast algorithm where the source says deliberately slow.

cases.text: it's the thing where the password gets turned into a random-looking string so it isn't stored as is. i think you can't really get it back? not totally sure
cases.notes: Right direction (not stored as-is, maybe irreversible) but one-way is only guessed at and fixed-length output and slow salting are absent.

cases.text: You lock the data up with a key so it's gibberish to everyone else, and whoever holds the right key can unlock it back to exactly what it was - unlike a hash, which you can't undo.
credits: A reversible transformation that protects data
cases.notes: Keyed, reversible protection of data, contrasted correctly with one-way hashing.

cases.text: Encryption is one-way: once the data is scrambled you can never get the original back, and that's exactly why it's secure.

misconceptions.claim: A reversible transformation that protects data

cases.notes: Describes a one-way transformation, which is hashing; the source says encryption is reversible with a key.

cases.text: scrambles your data so hackers can't read it
cases.notes: Right that it hides data, but says nothing about keys or getting the data back, which is the core of this concept.

cases.text: Encryption is why you should always look for the padlock and HTTPS in the address bar; websites without it aren't safe for typing in your card details.
cases.notes: Browser-safety advice that never says what encryption is or does.

cases.text: An index makes lookups on a column faster, because the database saves the answers of queries you've already run and hands them back instantly the next time.
credits: make particular lookups or orderings faster
cases.notes: Faster lookups is right, but the mechanism given is a query-result cache rather than a maintained structure that avoids scanning rows.

cases.text: Indexes = quicker searches. How it works: the DB remembers the results of previous queries, so the second time you ask it just returns the saved result.
credits: make particular lookups or orderings faster
cases.notes: Same right conclusion with the same wrong caching mechanism.

cases.text: It speeds up finding rows by a certain column. I believe it does that by caching results from earlier queries in memory, so repeated lookups skip the work.
credits: make particular lookups or orderings faster
cases.notes: Hedged version: speed-up is right, the reason (caching earlier results) is wrong.

cases.text: It's an extra structure the database keeps up to date so that searching or sorting by a particular column goes quicker.
credits: make particular lookups or orderings faster
cases.notes: Correct definition, but nothing about why it matters (large queries scanning huge numbers of rows otherwise).

cases.text: A closure is when you have a function inside another function. It has something to do with scope.
cases.notes: Names nesting and scope but not the key relationship: keeping access to the variables where the function was created.

cases.text: nested functions basically - a function defined in a function, and scope is involved somehow
cases.notes: Same pieces (nesting, scope) without saying what the inner function retains.

cases.text: I think it's about scope, like when one function is written inside of another one? That's a closure, I'm pretty sure.
cases.notes: Hedged restatement of nesting plus scope; the retained access to variables is missing.

cases.text: When the outer function finishes, all of its local variables get wiped, so the inner function can't see them anymore - a closure only works while the outer function is still running.

misconceptions.claim: after the outer function has finished.

cases.notes: The source says a closure keeps access to its lexical environment after the outer function has finished; this says the opposite.

cases.text: The way I picture it, a function carries a little backpack holding the variables that were around where it was born, and it can keep using and even changing them long after that outer function has returned. That's honestly the whole trick behind a lot of stuff - private counters nobody else can touch, callbacks that remember things, React hooks, hiding data inside a module, all of that.
credits: access to the lexical variables from the scope
encapsulation, callbacks, hooks, and private state patterns.
cases.notes: Backpack analogy gives access to the creation-scope variables after the outer function returns, and lists the patterns closures power.

cases.text: It's like a takeaway counter where your order number is printed on your receipt: any cashier can serve you, because none of them has to remember you personally. The app box doesn't keep your session in its own RAM - that lives in a token or a shared store like Redis - so whichever copy gets your next call can handle it, which makes adding servers or surviving one dying way easier.
credits: without relying on request-specific state stored only
Any replica can serve the next request
cases.notes: Takeaway-counter analogy plus explanation: no per-request state in local memory, any copy can take the next call, easier scaling and failover.

cases.text: Each request carries or looks up everything it needs, so the server isn't holding on to per-user stuff in its own memory between calls.
credits: without relying on request-specific state stored only
cases.notes: Definition is right, but it never says why: any replica can serve the next request, easing scaling and failover.

cases.text: A stateless server doesn't store any data at all - no database, no sessions, nothing anywhere. Everything has to be worked out from scratch on every single request.

misconceptions.claim: keep request state outside a specific instance

cases.notes: Overgeneralizes 'stateless' to 'no state anywhere'; the source says state is kept outside the specific instance, not eliminated.

cases.text: Any instance can answer the next request, and that's because stateless servers are lighter and faster since they basically don't use memory.
credits: Any replica can serve the next request
cases.notes: Any-instance conclusion is right, but the reason (lighter, faster, no memory use) is wrong; it works because request state lives outside the instance.

cases.text: it has no state
cases.notes: Just restates the name; no sign of which state, where it lives, or why it matters.

cases.text: Instead of making one server beefier, you just add more servers running the same app.
credits: capacity by adding more instances or machines
cases.notes: Adding machines is right, but nothing about higher throughput or redundancy beyond one box.

cases.text: scaling out: spin up extra copies/machines rather than upgrading the one box you have
credits: capacity by adding more instances or machines
cases.notes: Same core idea (more copies, not a bigger box) with the benefit still missing.

cases.text: You grow by adding more machines to the pool - so you might go from a handful of instances to dozens of them.
credits: capacity by adding more instances or machines
cases.notes: Adds machines to grow capacity; no mention of throughput or resilience beyond one box.

cases.text: Horizontal scaling means upgrading your server - more RAM, a faster CPU - so the same machine can handle more users.

misconceptions.claim: capacity by adding more instances or machines

cases.notes: Upgrading one machine's RAM/CPU is vertical scaling; horizontal adds more instances.

cases.text: Scaling up: you give the one machine a bigger CPU and more RAM, like swapping your laptop for a monster workstation. It's usually the easy first thing to try, but you can only buy so big a box, and if that single box goes down you're still down.
credits: Increasing the CPU, RAM, or resources
has hardware and availability limits
cases.notes: More resources for one machine, simplest first move, and both the hardware ceiling and the availability limit.

cases.text: Vertical scaling is just upgrading your server's hardware, and it's the best approach because there's no ceiling - you can keep adding RAM forever - and having one really powerful machine gets rid of the single point of failure.

misconceptions.claim: has hardware and availability limits
can preserve a single point of failure

credits: Increasing the CPU, RAM, or resources
cases.notes: Definition right, but claims no limits and that one big box removes the single point of failure - both contradict the source.

cases.text: making the server bigger i guess?
cases.notes: A hedged, vague 'bigger'; the one-machine resource idea is only gestured at and the limits are absent.

cases.text: It's like a festival wristband: your app shows it on every API call to prove it's allowed in, and it's only good until tonight, so if somebody swipes it they don't get to use it for long.
credits: credential presented to an API to authorize
reduce damage if the token is stolen
cases.notes: Wristband analogy covers presenting it on each API call, a short lifetime, and why short limits damage if stolen.

cases.text: the short-lived thing you send in the Authorization header whenever you call an API
credits: credential presented to an API to authorize
cases.notes: What it is and that it is short-lived are right, but not why the lifetime is short (limiting damage if stolen).

cases.text: An access token is the long-lasting one you keep for weeks and use to get new tokens without logging in again. Making it last longer is actually safer, since you're not sending your password around.

misconceptions.claim: usually with a relatively short lifetime
reduce damage if the token is stolen

cases.notes: Describes the refresh token (long-lived, used to get new tokens) and claims longer lifetimes are safer, the opposite of the source.

cases.text: Tokens are used everywhere in modern apps - OAuth, OpenID Connect, 'Sign in with Google' and so on.
cases.notes: True-sounding name-dropping with nothing about what an access token is or why it is short-lived.

cases.text: A refresh token lets the app grab a fresh access token without making you log in again - it works because your password is saved inside it, so the server just logs you in again automatically.
credits: used to obtain new access tokens
cases.notes: Getting new access tokens without a new sign-in is right, but the mechanism (it contains your password) is invented.

cases.text: When the access token dies, the refresh token gets you a new one with no login screen. That's possible because the refresh token is basically your password in encrypted form, which the auth server re-checks each time.
credits: used to obtain new access tokens
cases.notes: Same right conclusion; same wrong reason (it is the user's stored password).

cases.text: It's what quietly gets you a new access token so you're not kicked back to sign-in; my understanding is it holds your username and password and just replays them.
credits: used to obtain new access tokens
cases.notes: Hedged version: right outcome, wrong credential-replay mechanism.

cases.text: it refreshes your login so you stay signed in, kind of? not sure how
cases.notes: Gestures at staying signed in but not that it obtains new access tokens, nor the convenience/short-lifetime balance.

cases.text: You cap how many calls each user or API key can make in a given window, say 100 a minute, and anything past that gets bounced with a 429.
credits: how frequently a client, identity, or key
cases.notes: Per-client cap on frequency is right; why (availability, cost, abuse) is missing.

cases.text: each client only gets so many requests per time period; go over and you're blocked for a bit
credits: how frequently a client, identity, or key
cases.notes: Same definition in casual words, still no purpose.

cases.text: Rate limiting is restricting how frequently a client, identity or key may perform an operation.
credits: how frequently a client, identity, or key
cases.notes: Near copy of the definition only; the purpose sentence is not expressed.

cases.text: i think it's kind of like a speed limit on how much people can use something? so it doesn't get overloaded maybe
cases.notes: Speed-limit image gestures at limiting use and avoiding overload, but not per client/key frequency; too vague to trust.

cases.text: It's the reason your phone plan slows your data down after you've used up your 20GB for the month.
cases.notes: Carrier data caps are a different thing; nothing about restricting how often a client may perform an operation.

cases.text: When a service keeps failing, the breaker cuts it off completely and your app stops calling it for good, until someone goes in and resets it by hand.

misconceptions.claim: a failure threshold, then probe recovery.

cases.notes: Says the cut-off is permanent until a manual reset; the source says calls stop temporarily and recovery is probed.

cases.text: It's a kill switch: enough errors and the dependency is permanently disconnected, and it stays that way until an engineer switches it back on.

misconceptions.claim: a failure threshold, then probe recovery.

cases.notes: Same wrong idea (permanent disconnect, no probing), stated assertively.

cases.text: after too many failures you just never call that service again. it's disabled, full stop, until a manual reset

misconceptions.claim: a failure threshold, then probe recovery.

cases.notes: Same permanent-cutoff belief in terse casual wording.

cases.text: After a bunch of failures in a row you stop sending calls to the broken service for a while, then let one test request through to see if it's back before opening the floodgates again.
credits: Stop calling a failing dependency temporarily
cases.notes: Threshold, temporary stop and probing are right, but not why: stopping slow failures from eating all resources.

cases.text: It stops calling a dependency that keeps failing and tries it again later. The point is that otherwise the failed responses would get cached and served to users.
credits: Stop calling a failing dependency temporarily
cases.notes: The behaviour is right, but the reason (avoiding cached error responses) is not the source's reason of protecting resources from repeated slow failures.

cases.text: You retry after the same fixed wait every time, like 2 seconds, 2 seconds, 2 seconds. And the jitter is what makes all the clients retry at exactly the same moment, so the server can deal with them in one go.

misconceptions.claim: where delays grow after consecutive failures,
prevents many clients from retrying in lockstep.

cases.notes: Two wrong ideas: delays stay fixed instead of growing, and jitter is said to synchronize clients, the reverse of what it does.

cases.text: So basically every time a retry fails you wait longer before the next attempt - like 1 second, then 2, then 4, then 8, roughly doubling each round - and you usually throw a little bit of randomness on top of each wait. That's the pattern, anyway; it's basically a smarter way of doing retries than just hammering the thing over and over again with the same wait each time.
credits: where delays grow after consecutive failures,
cases.notes: Growing delays with jitter are described well, but the purpose (breathing room for a recovering service, avoiding synchronized retry storms) stays vague.

cases.text: it's about retrying stuff but slower each time? something exponential, i don't fully get it
cases.notes: A hedged, vague 'slower each time'; the growing-delay idea is only gestured at, with no jitter or purpose.

cases.text: Exponential growth is when something keeps doubling, like compound interest or bacteria splitting in a petri dish.
cases.notes: True statement about exponential growth in general; nothing about retries, delays or protecting a recovering service.

cases.text: useMemo is for performance, it memoizes things so the app is faster.
cases.notes: Knows it is a performance tool but not what is cached (a calculation result) or when it is recomputed (dependencies change).

cases.text: It's an optimization hook - you wrap stuff in it to make React quicker, something to do with memo.
cases.notes: Same pieces (optimization, memo) without the cache-until-dependencies-change relationship.

cases.text: i think it's used to speed up components, like memoization? so things don't slow down
cases.notes: Hedged version of the same vague speed-up idea.

cases.text: useMemo guarantees your function will never run again unless the dependencies change, so you can rely on it to make sure side effects only happen once.

misconceptions.claim: a performance optimization, not a semantic guarantee.

cases.notes: Treats useMemo as a hard guarantee to rely on for correctness; the source says it is only a performance optimization.

cases.text: It's a React hook.
cases.notes: True but says nothing about what it caches or why.

cases.text: It hands you back the same function object across renders as long as the deps don't change. That matters when you pass the function down to a child wrapped in React.memo, or when it sits in a useEffect dependency list - otherwise you'd get a brand-new function every render, which would re-render the child or re-run the effect for no reason, which is kind of the whole point.
credits: caches a function reference until dependencies change.
matter for memoized children or effect dependencies.
cases.notes: Same function reference until deps change, and why that identity matters for memoized children and effect dependencies.

cases.text: useCallback runs your function and caches whatever it returns, so the expensive computation doesn't happen again on each render.

misconceptions.claim: caches a function reference until dependencies change.

cases.notes: Caching the returned value of a computation is useMemo; useCallback caches the function reference itself.

cases.text: useCallback keeps the same function reference between renders until the deps change - it does that so the function executes faster, since React doesn't have to compile it again each time.
credits: caches a function reference until dependencies change.
cases.notes: Definition is right, but the reason (faster execution, no recompiling) is invented; stable identity matters for memoized children and effects.

cases.text: A React hook that caches a function reference until dependencies change.
credits: caches a function reference until dependencies change.
cases.notes: Copies the definition but gives no reason why a stable function identity matters.

cases.text: A controlled component is an input that keeps its own value in the DOM, and you read it with a ref when the form gets submitted.

misconceptions.claim: current value is driven by React state/props.

cases.notes: DOM-owned value read through a ref is the uncontrolled pattern; a controlled element's value is driven by React state/props.

cases.text: The box shows whatever is in state, and typing fires onChange which updates that state - so React always decides what's displayed in the input.
credits: current value is driven by React state/props.
cases.notes: State drives the value and changes flow back through events, but the purpose (validation, formatting, coordinated UI) is missing.

cases.text: you use value and onChange on the input, i think that's what makes it controlled?

cases.text: The API just drops the task onto the queue and a worker handles it later, so the user gets a quick response instead of waiting for the email to go out. The reason that's faster, as far as I know, is that queues talk over a special binary protocol that's way lighter than HTTP, so the work itself takes less time to do - which is why every big company uses them.
credits: producers enqueue messages/jobs and consumers process them later.
cases.notes: Enqueue-then-worker and the quick response are right, but the explanation (a lighter binary protocol makes the work faster) is a non-sequitur; the gain comes from decoupling.

cases.text: Pick the array method by what you want out of it - one item (find), a new array (filter) or a true/false (some/every). And if you get back a true/false you can't chain .map() onto it.

boolean cannot be followed by .map().
cases.notes: Choose by the return shape you need, and a boolean result cannot be chained with .map().

cases.text: It's like ordering food: decide whether you want one dish, a whole platter or just a yes/no answer before you pick the menu item. If the method hands you a plain yes/no, you can't carry on with .map() because that only exists on arrays.
credits: starts with the shape you need back.
boolean cannot be followed by .map().

cases.text: A component is basically a recipe for what the UI should look like given its props, state and context. Rendering is React working out that recipe; committing is the separate step where it actually touches the screen, and only with the changes that are needed.
credits: describes the interface for a particular set
Rendering calculates that description;
applies the necessary changes to the screen.
cases.notes: All three ideas: component as a description for given inputs, rendering computes it, committing applies only needed changes.

cases.text: Rendering is obviously when React paints the changes onto the screen, and committing is the step before that where it figures out what the component should look like.

misconceptions.claim: Rendering calculates that description;

cases.notes: Swaps the two phases: the source says rendering calculates the description and committing applies changes to the screen.
